speechtext: The hon. member for New Westminster had given me notice of his intention to ask part of this question. Whatever action Canada has taken by way of representations would not be as a member of the commission. The commission has its prescribed functions. But the government has been in consultation with most of the governments participating in the Geneva conference, and in particular we have noted press reports of the proposed joint action to be taken by the governments of the Soviet union and France. The precise proposal, however, has not been put before us. When that is done we will give it the consideration which this critical and important situation requires. We have already made it clear that once there is an easing of tension, and a cessation of hostilities, consideration can be given to the steps which could be taken to try to provide for some stability in that area.

speechtext: I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Labour. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Fisheries. In view of the recent announcement by the minister regarding the killing of seals, would he advise the house whether steps have been or will be taken to see that helicopters and other aircraft will

Inquiries of the Ministry not be permitted to fly over seal herds during the whelping period, thereby giving protection to the mother seals while their young are being born?

speakeroldname: Hon. H. J. Robichaud (Minister of Fisheries):
subtopic: SEALS-USE OF AIRCRAFT DURING WHELPING PERIOD

should like to address a question to the Minister of Justice. Some time ago the minister announced to the house that he was setting

up a special committee to investigate the distribution of hate literature. I would ask him whether this committee has been set up and, if so, when he expects it to report to the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: HATE LITERATURE-APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE-REPORT OF BOARD OF REVIEW
speechtext: I am pleased to inform the house that a committee has been formed headed by Dean Maxwell Cohen of the McGill University law school and composed of many well known students of civil liberties and matters connected therewith throughout Canada. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Justice. maintopic: DORION COMMISSION-LEAKAGE OF INFORMATION IN SECRET POLICE REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think I can allow the words of the hon. member to go unchallenged.

maintopic: DORION COMMISSION-LEAKAGE OF INFORMATION IN SECRET POLICE REPORT
speechtext:
Oh, oh.
Inquiries of the Ministry

maintopic: DORION COMMISSION-LEAKAGE OF INFORMATION IN SECRET POLICE REPORT
speechtext: I raise this matter on a question of privilege. The hon. member for Renfrew South has used the word "stolen". That was the purport of his remarks, and if he did mean that I would ask you, sir, to require the hon. member to withdraw that word.

maintopic: DORION COMMISSION-LEAKAGE OF INFORMATION IN SECRET POLICE REPORT

I made no implication that the hon. member stole the report or illegally obtained the information. I requested information as to how he got information from a report which was apparently stolen or otherwise illegally obtained.

maintopic: DORION COMMISSION-LEAKAGE OF INFORMATION IN SECRET POLICE REPORT

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, February 24, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-136, to establish a comprehensive program of old age pensions and supplementary benefits in Canada payable to and in respect of contributors-Miss LaMarsh-Mr. Lamou-reux in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Order. House again in committee of the whole on Bill No. C-136. When the committee rose last evening the committee was discussing clause 2 and an amendment thereto by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka.
On clause 2-Definitions.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee terminated at six o'clock last night I was in the course of making a few remarks on this bill, and in particular on the amendment offered by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. I have subsequently had the opportunity to review in Hansard the remarks made by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, and I wish to congratulate him on stating quite forthrightly the amendments which are to be proposed by the party to which he belongs in this house. Therefore I will not take too much time of the committee in concluding my remarks.
On the face of it, we have an amendment which adds a definition of "resident" to clause 2 of the bill. It appears an innocent amendment, but as the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka indicated it is the purpose of his group to move subsequent amendments which, if adopted, could really have the effect of changing the character of the bill so fundamentally as, in my opinion, to destroy it.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka quite frankly told us, as reported at page 11702 of Hansard:
However, we intend to propose later on certain substantive amendments to various clauses which would add as beneficiairies persons who will have made a smaller contribution than the one envisaged or, in some cases, no contribution at all to the fund.
It was pointed out to the hon. member in the course of the proceedings of the special joint committee of this house and the other place which was appointed to consider this bill that this type of amendment could open the door to a number of abuses if control was not exercised. The kind of abuse which was suggested would be, for example, for a
Canada Pension Plan
resident of the city of Detroit who lives across the border from Windsor to come to Canada and qualify for a Canada pension plan minimum pension with very little difficulty.
Quite frankly, it is with the purpose of trying to rule out that type of claim that this amendment is offered. In fact the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka said this was why they were moving to bring into this particular clause a residential requirement, because he did not feel that a person should be entitled to come to Canada from another country and take advantage of our minimum pension legislation. This is indicative of the way in which the hon. member seeks to open up the entire legislation and the fund itself.
The submission from the province of Ontario pointed out that no fewer than six federal-provincial conferences had considered this legislation. In addition there were a number of exchanges of correspondence between the premier of the province of Ontario and the Prime Minister of Canada on the subject. This amendment and the others which were outlined by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka would have the effect of referring the whole bill back to a federal-provincial conference and would call for another series of wide ranging discussions. In one breath hon. members on the other side say that so far we have had two or even three versions of the Canada pension plan, and ask how many more there will be. Then, Mr. Chairman, they offer an amendment which would call for many more versions if the legislation were to survive.
Mr. Chairman, one aspect of this amendment gives me a great deal of concern. I touched upon that aspect briefly yesterday. We asked the hon. members who were making this suggestion whether they would advocate paying this extra $25 per month to the recipients of old age security right across the country. Of course the answer was that the benefit would be paid only in those provinces where the funds were being raised. That would mean that Canada would be divided into nine provinces in which the $25 supplement would be paid, and the tenth province where the federal government would not pay that supplement to the recipients of old age security. In that event, discussions with the tenth province would have to take place in order to determine just exactly what would happen. I cannot think of any manoeuvre that could be more cynically designed to split and divide Canada.
The effect of these amendments, suggested by the hon. member would be essentially the

Canada Pension Plan
transferring of a program which is financed by payroll taxes into a universal benefit type of program, substantially reducing the graduated scale of pension, and it would take a recipient 20 years to reach the maximum rather than ten years.
We now have an old age security program on our books which is financed through a combination of personal and corporation income tax and sales tax. This is the so-called 4-3-3 formula. It is very interesting to observe what the hon. members on the other side of this house had in mind. They accuse us of giving huge bonuses to the wealthy, but let us look at what their proposal would do. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka said that after his amendment had been adopted there would be an estimated surplus of $75 million to $100 million per year, but only after $107 million had been raised through a new type of tax.
Let us look at the kind of taxing method he has in mind. Under his system an individual who earns $600 or less would not pay any contributions. I have some calculations which I should like to place on the record, Mr. Chairman. At the present time one who earned $600 would not pay a contribution under the proposal which the government has placed before this house. That individual would not pay anything on the $600 under the proposal suggested by the hon. member. However, as soon as that individual earned $1 more than the $600 he would pay $10.80 as his share, and the employer would pay an equal amount.
Let us consider an individual who earned $1,000 per year. Under the terms of the bill now before us he would pay $7.20, but under the proposal outlined by the hon. member yesterday that individual would pay $18, or an increase of 150 per cent in his contributions.
Let us consider an individual earning $2,000 per year. Under the proposal now before the house he would pay $25.20, but under the amendment proposed by the hon. member he would pay $36, or an increase of 43 per cent.
An individual earning $3,000 under the government proposal would pay 25 per cent less than under the hon. member's proposal. An individual earning $4,000 would pay contributions to the extent of 17.6 per cent more under the hon. member's proposal than under the proposal placed before the house by the government. The increase would be 13.6 per cent in respect of an income of $5,000 under the terms of the hon. member's proposal.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, an individual earning $1,000 per year would pay 150
IMr. Francis.]
per cent more in contributions under the hon. member's proposal than under the government's proposal, but an individual earning $5,000 per year would pay an increase of only 13.6 per cent. This proposal is suggested by an hon. member of that party which accuses us of giving too much to the wealthy groups and not enough to the poor. The tax structure suggested by the hon. member proposes the raising of another $107 million to keep the fund solvent.
I suggest to this house that the amendment proposed by the hon. member is only the first of a series of irresponsible amendments motivated purely by political considerations to support this great cry that we should give the most at the earliest possible age. It would be a tragedy not only for the elderly people of Canada but for all Canadians if that philosophy became the basis upon which successive parties or members of this house made decisions in respect of the levels of pensions. This would have the effect of destroying the funding principle. The hon. member's proposal would save the fund only through the imposition of regressive taxes, and for that reason, Mr. Chairman, I believe the amendment as proposed by the hon. member, as well as the subsequent amendments which the hon. member has indicated are to be proposed, are so fundamental in character that they would destroy the bill itself.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka was quite forthright in telling the committee that the amendment he proposed to clause 2, while it may seem to be a very simple one, is nevertheless part of a package his party wishes to propose as a general amendment to the bill now before us. Like the hon. member for Carleton, I therefore feel it is necessary to look at this amendment not only with an eye to its exact and limited wording, but with an eye to the total package which the Progressive Conservative party is going to propose.
Let me also say that in my view the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka presented his party's package in very clear terms. He has not tried to mislead us in any way. I believe, nevertheless, there are certain consequences which flow from the package offered by the Progressive Conservative party which make it terribly undesirable. I shall oppose the package as a whole; therefore I shall oppose the amendment to clause 2, which is that party's first step.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka has made quite clear, both in this house and outside of it, what his party proposes, namely that there be a $25 supplementary payment to individuals now drawing old age security, but that this supplementary payment be paid to them out of the Canada pension fund. This is not an increase in old age security payments under the Old Age Security Act. Some of my Conservative friends may say that the result is the same for today's old age security recipients as would be the result of our proposal to increase the amount of the old age security pension to $100 per month. That is the point at which any similarity or parallel ends. The Progressive Conservatives, as I say, propose a $25 supplement out of the Canada pension fund to those now 70 and over.
Canada Pension Plan
The Progressive Conservatives propose also that people between 65 and 69, if they are retired-that is people who are now in that age bracket-will get a $25 supplement out of the Canada pension fund.
The next step in their proposal is this: Persons who are, let us say, 60, 62 or 63 now, when they reach 65 and start to draw something from the Canada pension plan, if that something is less than $25, shall be given a guaranteed floor of $25. I see the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka is nodding his head, so I am stating their position correctly.
I believe the fourth element in their plan on the benefit side is that any persons in the 20 and 30 age group or on up, who spend their working lives below the $600 level and who have filed income returns, shall be guaranteed $25 per month out of the Canada pension fund when they reach 65. If by that time, as will be the case, the old age security pension is universal at age 65, this seems to be guaranteeing to everybody from 65 on a total pension benefit of $100 per month, that is, $75 old age security and $25 out of the Canada pension fund.
People already are a bit confused, Mr. Chairman. They believe that what the Conservatives are proposing is the same as what we are proposing. What we are advocating is not their proposal at all, but a straight amendment to the Old Age Security Act under which we say the amount should be increased to $100 per month available at 65. The differences are several. First, there are the kinds of differences the hon. member for Carleton has mentioned. For example the Progressive Conservative plan imposes, in our view, charges on the Canada pension fund which would throw it completely out of gear. There were complaints before our committee by some people that there is a lack of relationship between the pension paid under this plan and the contributions made to it. Well, that relationship would be completely destroyed if the fund, and I choose my words carefully, were raided in this way.
There are other complaints of that sort. I feel these amendments would call for another round of federal-provincial conferences which could well result in a loss of the Canada pension plan as we now have it. Somebody on television last night-yes, it was Don McGillivray-said the New Democratic party members are not satisfied with the plan, they do not think it is perfect, but it

Canada Pension Plan
goes a long way and therefore they do not want to lose it. Well, Don McGillivray is not far from the truth. This is our view. There are flaws in it, but we do not want to lose it. We are not going to support any package amendment that would result in that happening, and that is what the Conservative proposals would do to it.
My still greater concern about the package proposed by the Conservatives and my main complaint against it-I ask my friend the member for Parry Sound-Muskoka to listen carefully and when I get to some figures I have I will send him a copy of them-is that it will have the effect of paying people in the future a lower pension than they would get under Bill No. C-136. I will tell the committee in a moment which people they are. Some people may say, how can this happen when the Conservatives are proposing a $25 supplement? I will put the tables on the record in just a moment, but first let me explain how this comes about.
The Conservatives propose this supplement for people now 70 and over as well as the other groups to which I have referred, and in order to facilitate it they propose that the 10 year maturity period that is in Bill No. C-136 be changed to a 20 year maturity period. Now, do you see what that does to a person who is now 55 years of age? For example a person now 55 years of age who is at the $5,000 income level can expect under Bill No. C-136, at age 65 to receive a pension of $104 per month plus the $75 old age security, for a total of $179. However, if the Conservative package is put into effect and the maturity period becomes 20 years instead of 10, then the person now age 55, 10 years from now would get a pension out of the Canada pension plan of only $52 a month. This figure is above the $25 floor so he gets no benefit from the Conservative guarantee. In addition, he would receive the $75 old age security pension, so his total pension would be $127 per month, which is $52 less than the bill now provides.
This is what the Conservative plan will do. Every Canadian, therefore, who is today 55 years of age and over is going to get less when he retires at age 65 than he would get under this bill as it is now. I want to put these tables on the record in a moment, but I should like first to make this general comment. The fact is that everybody in Canada at the time the plan comes into existence, between the ages of 45 and 60, would get a lower pension on his retirement at age 65 under the Conservative plan than under the 
bill as it stands. Everybody between those two age limits would receive a lower pension.
In addition to that, many people above 60 would find themselves in the same situation. For example, people at the $5,000 level up to 62i years, would get a lower pension under the Conservative plan than they would get under Bill No. C-136 as it stands. My hon. friend from Parry Sound-Muskoka is quite honest about it. Quite frankly, this is what he wants to do. He is asking that there be a lower pension for those who will go on it in the next 10 or 15 years in order that we can use some of this money to pay a supplement to the people who are now 65 or over and to the people who are 70 years and over. We, in this party want more to be paid to our people over 65, and that is why we advocate that the old age security pension should be increased to $100 per month, payable at age 65. We say that if we are going to give a pension of $100 to people 70 and over and to people 65 and over, it should be paid for by everyone and paid for either out of the old age security tax or out of the general income tax assessed on the basis of ability to pay.
My hon. friends to the right would pay for this supplement they would give to people now 70 and over and to people between 65 and 70, by taking it out of the pensions of those Canadians contributing to the fund who are now between the ages of 45 and 62J. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that that is unfair to Canadians between 45 and 62J on two counts. First it would give them a lower pension than they would get under the bill as it stands and, second, it makes a particular group of people in Canada pay the shot for this proposal to increase the pension for those now retired. I submit therefore that a much more honest and equitable, much more sensible plan, to achieve the goal of $100 for people now 65 and over, is to do it directly in the way we are proposing, namely by amending the Old Age Security Act to increase the pension itself.
My hon. friend is concerned, and 1 share his concern, about people earning below $600. He proposes that they be brought in in the way he has indicated and that they be given a guaranteed $25 out of the Canada pension fund, even if they have not paid anything into it. Would it not be much better to give these people this extra $25 by increasing the old age security pension on a permanent basis from $75 to $100 per month. I am sure the hon. member agrees that I am stating the matter correctly, but some of the things that

have been said in this house by the hon. member tor Grey-Bruce and the hon. member for the Northwest Territories indicate that there is confusion, even in the minds of some members of the Conservative party, about this. I ask them to reconsider their whole position and to realize that if there is acceptance of the amendments the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka says are going to be put forward, the result will be a lower pension for all Canadians now between 45 and 60, and for many up to 62i, than would be provided under Bill No. C-136 as it stands.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I think hon. members should have a look at these figures. It had been my thought that we would not get to this until some days later, but perhaps it is just as well that the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka has raised the issue now because this means I can put on the record the tables I have prepared and hon. members can study these figures. In fact I hope in particular that members of the official opposition will study them and reconsider their position.

As I say, Mr. Chairman, hon. members may find it a bit surprising to learn that a scheme which talks about adding something to the pension has the actual effect of making reductions. Oftentimes we are asked where is the money to come from for some of the things we propose. We are asked that by Conservatives, and now they have given their answer regarding their proposals.
The Conservatives are going to pay the extra $25 to people aged 70, and to people who are retired now between the ages of 65 and 69, and they are going to $25 to people earning less than $600. To do this they have to get the money from somewhere, and where they are getting it is out of the pension which, under the terms of the bill would be payable to people now aged 45 to 62 when they reach the age of 65.
For the people who are below 45 years of age there is, of course, no difference. A person today aged 45 or 44, by the time he is 65 will benefit under the Tory 20 year maturity

plan to the extent of the full pension, and of course he gets the full pension anyway under the Liberal 10 year plan. In other words, for people under 45 years of age there is no difference. People above 70 years of age do better under the Conservative plan than under the Liberal plan, but for the great mass of Canadians between 45 and 62 years of age this package deal does them a great disservice.
As I say, I welcome the fact that the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka has given the house the whole package at this early stage. He gave it to us in the special committee and, as he knows, we voted against it in the committee for the very reasons which I have just outlined. However, I am glad he has given it now so that the figures I have referred to can be put on the record for members to study and see that this is not the way to deal with the problem.
Our position is well known. We contend that the old age security pension should be increased to $100 a month. We would leave the Canada pension plan contribution and benefit structure more or less as it is. We would like to have got rid of the $5,000 ceiling on contributions. I am sorry the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka had to make that correction in Hansard today; I thought he was going to get rid of the ceiling on contributions as well. There are certain other changes of that sort we would like, but in the main we believe the contribution and benefit structure in the plan is acceptable because it provides part of the old age pension package in relation to earnings and leaves the rest of the pension package on a flat rate basis. We think if we are going to try to improve the position of those who are now 70 or who will be 65 in the next three or four years, as well as of those who are now earning less than $600, the way to do it is not by providing a floor which later on you take away, which is what the Conservative party does, but by a straightforward increase in benefits under the Old Age Security Act itself.
I may say I do not like the proposal the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka makes that the $600 exemption level be removed as far as contributions are concerned. One of the things that is good about that exemption level is that it weights the contribution scale in favour of the low paid people. People with $1,000 or $2,000 do not pay as high a percentage of their total earnings as do the $4,000 and $5,000 people. I regard the re-
Canada Pension Plan
moval of the $600 exemption as a totally indefensible means of getting extra money and I will vote against it. This is the reason I am against the amendment to put in a residence clause. It is part of a package deal which has been clearly outlined to us by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, and I have pointed out that it worsens the whole arrangement instead of bettering it and I ask my friends in the Conservative party to take another look at it. My hon. friend and his friends believe something should be done for those who are 70 and over. They argue that the legislation should be made more simple. But they have done something to make it more complicated. I suggest that in view of their interest in seeing that things are simplified they should abandon the proposal they have made and support us in asking for a straight increase in old age security benefits to $100 a month. Inasmuch as the plan put forward by the hon. member worsens the picture and would mean lower pensions for people now between the ages of 45 and 62, we shall have to vote against all aspects of these proposals.

Would the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre permit a question? I think he is a fair minded man. I think he said that all Canadians in the age bracket between 45 and 62 would be worse off under our plan?

Why did he use people in the three categories $5,000, $3,600 and $2,400 per annum? Why did he stop there? Why did he not go further down to the man who needs it most, the man earning $1,000? He gets more under our plan. Everyone earning less than $1,000 gets more under our plan.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
In practical terms, surely in the next 20 or 30 years there will not be people down in those lower brackets. If the hon. member and his friends are thinking in terms of that kind of an economy I suggest, there is some other place for them than in the parliament of Canada. I picked figures which I thought were representative and just as low as we ought to contemplate. To me, $200 is a starvation wage and we should not be thinking in terms of a pension plan being necessary for people below that figure. There ought not to be any such people. I picked not only the $5,000 level, which is the standard one; I picked also the reasonably low figures of $300 and $200 a month which, I suggest, repre-

Canada Pension Plan
sent a true picture of our people across the board. It is these people, the great mass of Canadians, who would have their pensions reduced if the Conservative package were accepted.
I should like to ask the hon. member how he proposes to raise the $455 million a year that his proposal would cost.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka was straightforward in letting the house know the source from which his party would get the money to pay for their plan. They would get it by postponing the benefits available to people now aged between 45 and 62, by removing the $600 exemption level and so on. I accept that as being the position of the hon. member, though I do not agree with it. We propose that the extra money needed to pay higher pensions under the Old Age Security Act would be obtained by general taxation either under the old age security 4-3-3 formula or by amending the Income Tax Act. We would remove the $3,000 ceiling on income tax payments into the old age security fund so that people in the brackets above $3,000 taxable income would pay their share of the total cost. A capital gains tax and other taxes are possible methods, but we think the cost of paying increased old age pensions should be borne by the whole community on the basis of ability to pay, by graduated income tax, and not by charging a select group between 45 and 62 as the Conservative members propose to do.

Is it not a fact that the proposals the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has made might result in an increase in personal income tax of approximately 23 per cent, according to the evidence which was given before the committee?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I have the figures which were given to us in the committee. I do not know whether the hon. member is talking about 23 percentage points or 23 per cent of the income tax now being paid, but it would all depend on whether there was a flat rate tax or whether you graduated the increase. I favour a graduated increase. But the hon. member's question is one which has been asked since the earliest days when old age pensions were first contemplated. Even when the pension was to be only $20 there were people who said we would never be able to afford it. We were told we could not raise the amount, that we could not abolish the means test. But we have managed to do so, and just as I think we can afford a Canada

pension plan which provides for a maximum pension of $104, so we can afford an old age security plan providing for $100 and enable all our people to enjoy the security and dignity in retirement which the government and others like to talk about.

The hon. member spoke of taking the cost from the fund. Did he mean the pension fund-the fund required to pay these pensions under the pension plan? Or was he referring to the huge investment funds that are supposed to be built up as a result of the operations of this plan?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I hope I did not make anything less than clear. I did not propose that any of the funds necessary to pay increased old age security benefits should be taken from the Canada pension plan fund. I said the money should be obtained either in the same way as old age security money is presently raised, or through general taxation. I do not think you should take out of the Canada pension plan fund, which has been devised as an earnings-related scheme, funds for adding to flat rate benefits. We have made our criticism, and it still stands, about the level of contribution that is required. Our criticism is that too much of this money from low paid people is to go into a fund which will be lent to the provinces. But two wrongs do not make a right. Money which we think should not be collected for lending to the provinces should likewise not be used to pay flat rate benefits. I am asking that the money necessary to pay adequate old age security benefits should be raised from all the people of Canada through old age security taxation, through general taxation on a graduated basis and by means of a capital gains tax, not by a levy against a particular age group.
Would the hon. member not agree that the 1.8 per cent contribution which is to be derived from industry across the country is not a direct tax on industry?

Mr. Chairman, I did not intend to speak again, but after hearing the hon. member for Carleton last night and today I thought I should say a few words. I am also pleased to have heard the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, because I am now beginning to realize how the minds of these socialists work.
The hon. member said that the man 55 years of age who pays in for ten years and whose average earnings have been $5,000 a year minimum-it might have been $50,000 a year-arrives at a pension, under the Canada pension plan proposed by the government, of $104 a month, and under our proposal it would be $52 a month. That is the man the hon. member is supporting; but the people earning under $1,000, on the average, do not concern him. In his mind, they do not exist. These are the people we are trying to help, the people who are in the greatest need. It is not an instrument by which we are heading an attack on rural poverty. As reported on page 11704 of Hansard, the hon. member for Carleton apparently decried our proposal and said it would also have very serious effects on the nature of the fund itself. Subsequent to the introduction of this bill

-the federal government proposed to introduce a universal old age pension. regard to a resident. May I point out to him and all hon. members of the committee that the Canada pension plan itself has no residence requirement; a man could come from some foreign country and reside here for two years-
From South Africa.

Mr. Chairman, before the vote is taken on this particular clause I think a few words by way of reply are due to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. In the first place I have not, of course, had a chance to check his figures, and since he says they are his own I will at least credit him with an effort to produce good, honest figures. I will of course go no further than that, because as everyone knows, not having the facilities which are available to the government we can only do the best we can with our estimates.

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit one question?
Yes.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: If when he checks my figures in Hansard tomorrow he finds any errors, will he publicly point them out?

Certainly I will point them out. What the hon. member has not pointed out in his statement to the committee is that his proposal would require additional taxation starting in 1966 of roughly $455 million per annum, which amount would be assessed against the people of Canada. At the same time he would be permitting the Canada pension plan fund to build up, yet not make any use of the funds which are available. In other words, he is proposing that the people of Canada should pay an extra sum by way of general taxation amounting to something of the order of $455 million.
The second matter is that he suggested that our proposals are cynical; at least, someone suggested that, perhaps not the hon. member. However, I say this about the hon. member's plan, that while our proposal deals with the Canada pension plan, he is attempting to do something which he knows very well is legally impossible under the bill as it is now proposed. The funds which he would have to raise under his plan would require a resolution to bring in changes to old age security. This is legally impossible for a private member, because when the hon. member gets to part IV of the bill he will having nothing to hang his hat on.
We feel, Mr. Chairman, that our proposal is within the confines of the Canada pension plan and payable from its fund; and that without changing the nature of the plan we will be able to bring benefits to those people who need them the most, and that we will be able to redistribute the funds in a much more equitable way. I agree that, if we were to adopt his figures and raise another $455 million per year by way of taxation, some people would be better off; I do not know how one could expect otherwise. But I still say that his proposal calls for increased taxation, and in addition is legally impossible under the bill before us.
We admit that by extending the transition period of this plan beyond 10 years certain persons in the higher income groups aged 55 and over will not benefit by the windfall which this plan provides. Those people with $5,000 income and aged 55 will under the present plan be able to pay in something like $900 and draw out a pension worth something between $16,000 to $18,000 at present values. We are proposing that this windfall be reduced and the money thereby saved 20220-742
Canada Pension Plan
used to provide a minimum pension of $25 a month for the man who otherwise might only receive $8.75 a month or $14.20, or some such figure.
In addition, those people in the marginal area around $600 a year will also receive a minimum pension. Many of these people may earn $600 to $1,000 this year, but perhaps next year are down below $600. Under the present plan they draw nothing, they are left out in the cold. Their total lifetime earnings will be so low that it would not be worth the effort. We contend that these people who earn under $600 will have such difficulty in paying the premium that we are not even going to collect it from them. We are going to collect it from the people in the higher income brackets and use those funds to pay a minimum pension of $25 to everyone regardless of the size of their income. Therefore I make no apology whatever for some of the figures which have been quoted indicating the windfall which the rich people in the older age groups, the people with good incomes, may receive. I also make no apology for seeking to reduce these windfalls, giving the benefits of them to those people in the very small income groups.

Mr. Chairman, I only have a few remarks to make, because, like you, I see that we are looking into the revised version of the tower of Babel of modern times.
Advocates of socialism represented by an expert in planning were heard respecting Bill No. C-136 and the proposed amendment.
On many occasions, we were told about the Liberal plan, the Conservative plan and the N.D.P. plan but those planners do not seem to agree too much among themselves.
The technocrats or mathematicians who came up with those figures to establish a pension plan seem to have second thoughts about them and to feel now that the old age security allowance should be increased. It is now being argued right and left that the old age pension should be raised to $100 or $125 as we have been advocating for a long time. Today, everyone seems to feel that this minimum of $75 a month should be increased to $100 as soon as possible whereas, only a year ago, it was felt that the $10 boost to raise the pension from $65 to $75 was quite generous.
As for the amendment under consideration, it bears witness to the complexity of this bill. Even experts who examined Bill No. C-136

Canada Pension Plan
during 51 meetings each have their own interpretation of the revised scheme.
What will result from that? There is talk of using the money paid into the fund by the contributors to put into force the plan proposed in Bill No. C-136. Others propose an increase in the old age security pension.
In closing, I would say that instead this pension scheme will get its funds from those who do not have enough already, because it is a plan that taxes poverty. Why? To entertain a host of civil servants who will play at mathematicians.

The purpose of this bill has, I believe, already been referred to in the house. It is to incorporate a pipe line which will carry gas liquids from western Alberta to tidewater on the west coast. It is new in principle. It is neither an oil line conflicting with existing oil lines carrying crude oil, nor is it a gas line in the sense that it carries combustible gas. It is for the purpose of carrying those elements of wet gases which are used in the petrochemical industry for the manufacture of paints, explosives, plastics and chemicals of many kinds. It is a high pressure line and its object is to bring these liquid gases through under pressure and refrigeration to export them to world markets.
I understand from those who are asking for the incorporation of this company that as soon as the bill carries they will be able to go ahead with the financing of this line. It will result in the building of a line of approximately 600 miles to the west coast. During construction, something in the neighbourhood of 1,800 men will be employed and a working force in the neighbourhood of 125 employees will be needed after the line is completed. By making use of the liquid elements of gases which are now merely running to consumers in the United States in some of these combustible gases, it is proposed to create a new secondary industry in western Canada with plants and developments both in Alberta and British Columbia.
Those who are asking for this incorporation are responsible citizens of Canada with 20220-742J

This is a company which is in very responsible hands and will bring to Canada a new secondary industry.

speechtext:
I shall be glad to do so. The purpose of this bill is to wind up a company which was incorporated by an act of parliament back in 1910. The present owners of the company are the three communities on the north shore in Vancouver, North Vancouver city, the district of north Vancouver and the district of west Vancouver. Within recent years they have sold this bridge, formerly known as the Second Narrows bridge and which is now paralleled by a new highway bridge, to Canadian National Railways. This is now a shell of a company. The assets are held in the form of Canada savings bonds. The municipalities would like to have these savings to invest in other municipal enterprises. The company, therefore, is being wound up by this act of parliament.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.
The house resumed from Thursday, November 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Basford for the second reading of Bill No. S-13, to incorporate Laurentide bank of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, before the Christmas recess, we dealt on several occasions with Bill No. S-13 providing for the establishment of a bank to be called the Laurentide bank of Canada. At that time we heard several members of the house wondering whether it was really necessary to grant additional bank charters in Canada.
As a matter of fact, since we received the Porter report after the government indicated its intention to revise the Bank Act, such

revision to be effected during 1965, I feel it would be in order that the promoters of new banks withdraw their project so as not to increase the confusion already existing.
We were able to read in the various reports of the standing committee on banking and commerce the evidence given by the main promoter of this project, Mr. Saunders.
It is interesting to note the exceedingly fast growth of the Laurentide Finance Company owned by Mr. Saunders and other associates.
I think it is also interesting to know that at one time Mr. Saunders recognized that in 1950 when he founded the Laurentide Finance Company, he had only $1,500 and that today, in 1964, at the time he was giving evidence, he had assets of $35 million.
Of course, you may say that money was invested in the business and that it is not only the initial $1,500 that produced such a phenomenal increase in the assets. We recognize that, but we are led to ask ourselves other questions. Why does the Laurentide Finance Company wish to have a bank charter since that finance company is already doing wonders?
It is very interesting to note that when he appeared before the committee, as may be seen on page 10 of report No. 1 dated May 27, 1964, Mr. Saunders said:
It is because they were convinced-
He referred to the promoters of this project.
-and they still are, that such an establishment would be very profitable for our company-
Their company.
.-at the same time, benefits could be derived and their relations could be mutually profitable.
I can only agree with him and recognize that a bank would be of a great assistance to them. To show to what extent that could help them to get credit funds enabling them to borrow money at a small rate of interest to lend it back at a rate of 2 per cent per month, I should like to draw the attention of hon. members of the committee to a few words reported on page 129 of the report of the royal commission on banking and finance. We read on page 114 of this report tabled last year:
About 30 per cent of the bank's authorized lines of credit of $100,000 or more at the end of 1962 were to directors, their firms, or corporations of which they were officers or directors, or were guaranteed by them.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that this simple sentence defines the main reason why the

promoters and present owners of the Lau-rentide Finance wish to have their own bank.
It is obvious that under those conditions these people, with the credit and the capacity to multiply credit enjoyed by a chartered bank, will have at their disposal fantastic sums which they will lend at a rate of interest known to all, 1J or 2 per cent per month. They want a bank not for banking operations but to have sources of credit and money to finance their own finance company which has now branches throughout the country.
This company, the Laurentide, has opened an office in my own town of Alma, where there are already too many finance companies, and I have been told that it chose the former site of the Bank of Montreal because it is well located, it is known as a place where many business transactions have taken place, and if it turns out that the Laurentide Finance obtains its charter for a bank, it could use that branch for its Laurentide Bank.
You can picture the situation. Someone goes to the bank wicket to obtain a loan and is referred to another wicket.
The teller goes to another wicket, borrows money from the bank at 6 per cent interest and then lends it to me at 24 per cent interest. Of course that saves us a few steps, there is no need to cross the street.
Today there is a bank and a finance company facing each other on opposite sides of the street. The bank refuses to grant us a loan and advises us to see a finance company across the street. If the idea is to save steps, the best thing is to have everything under the same roof, the bank and the finance company, to save time.
On the other hand, the time is ill-chosen to authorize new chartered banks. We have that commission's report and we know also that the government intends to amend the chartered bank legislation every ten years, although that is already a year overdue. Therefore, in these circumstances, I think it would be advisable to wait another year before reviewing those applications for chartered banks.
Mr. Speaker, it is also important to note the interest shown by honourable senators in the banking and commerce committee with regard to this proposal; they were extremely interested. Of course most of them are bank and finance company directors. Therefore, they were extremely interested in that proposal and they asked probing questions to all the witnesses appearing before

the committee, and to Mr. Saunders in particular.
These gentlemen wanted to make sure that there would not be any competition with their own businesses. They also wanted to make sure that they would be able to buy shares of that concern. In fact, the questions asked showed their interest-

You made your own comments last year, and I think that you were allowed complete freedom of speech. Now let me express my opinion.
Mr. Speaker, if one considers the questions asked and the answers recorded in the proceedings I have in my hand, one sees that the senators who attended the meeting were strangely interested in finding out what was advocated in respect to the incorporation of this bank.
This also leads us to ask ourselves another question. Why did the senators deem it advisable to concur in the proposal of the Laurentide bank of Canada, as well as that of the bank of western Canada, while refusing the proposals of the government of British Columbia?
They claimed that it was excessively dangerous to allow a government to invest in a bank.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that it is no more dangerous to let a government invest in a bank than to let individuals do so, since the individuals who now request the establishment of a chartered bank, in brief the promoters of the Laurentide bank of Canada, have certainly some personal interests to protect.
When they appeared before the committee, they gave evidence that it is for their own interest that they want to establish chartered banks. In fact, Mr. Saunders himself stated that in the interest of shareholders, what they want is a deal.
Mr. Speaker, if it is dangerous to let a provincial government hold shares in a banking business, I feel that it is just as dangerous to allow any individual in this country to do so.
If the Senate felt justified to recommend to the house the granting of a charter to the Laurentide bank of Canada and the bank of

western Canada, it should also have recommended the taking into consideration of the request for incorporation of a bank in British Columbia. I am not opposing the incorporation of the Laurentide bank of Canada merely because the request of the province of British Columbia was turned down. I feel that the basis of preference used in three cases was unfair, and justifies my opposition.
In my opinion, the house should continue refusing to pass any of those bills during the remainder of this session. The whole question should be shelved until we have had a chance to examine the proposals the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) intends to put before us concerning the amendments to the Bank Act.
It is only after the decennial revision of this legislation has taken place that we shall be able to decide whether it is advisable to grant charters to other banking interests in our country.

Mr. Speaker, we still have a few remarks to make concerning Bill No. S-13, not because we are opposed to the creation of new banks in Canada, not because we are against new banks, but rather because we are opposed to the means they use to aggravate Canada's economic position.
We feel that we have an adequate number of banks in Canada at the present time.
I feel also that we have enough bogus money circulating in Canada at present, that we should not establish other banks that would create still more.
Mr. Speaker, another application for a bank charter is placed before us. It is very difficult to refuse honourable Canadians the privilege of creating new institutions which would benefit them, and all the Canadian people at the same time, as is the case in all other types of production or service.
If a farmer produces foodstuffs, it is certainly for himself and at the same time to help other people. If a carpenter builds houses, it is certainly to earn money, it is for himself, but it is also to render a service to others, to those who need housing. So it is for all trades and professions.
But if chartered banks restricted themselves to rendering such services as loans, exchange, administering public and company savings, we would not object to an increase in their number as far as it may be needed.
But in the case of banks, as they now exist, with their credit creating privilege, even on the guarantee of borrowers and governments, in the case of banks, precisely because they perform a part of the duties of the Bank of

Canada, that of creating the money needed for the movement of goods and services in Canada, we object to the incorporation of new banks that would issue new money, new credit, and we propose that all those issues of new credit, new money, be made exclusively by the bank of the people, for the benefit of the people.
Nowadays it is useless and harmful to multiply banks which are in competition with the Bank of Canada for the issuance of money or credit used as money.
Mr. Speaker, I am not expressing an opinion, I am not preaching a new doctrine, I merely give facts. I am pointing out an obvious evil, a permanent evil, an evil which undermines all financial structures in Canada. This evil is the national privilege of creating money granted to individuals in Canada who may use that privilege for their own benefit, whereas the Bank of Canada is, or should be, the only one to have such a privilege, in the name of Canada as a whole and for the benefit of all Canadian citizens.
Last year, for instance, the Bank of Canada had a net profit of $116 million, which it turned over to the Minister of Finance of Canada, whereas all other banks distributed their profits to stockholders and saw their shares go up from $10 to $80 between 1944 and 1964. Who is profiting by that? The people or the stockholders?
Once again, let companies and banks make profits, we are not against that. But the fact that banks are given the privilege of creating credit money, the fact that this privilege is given exclusively to the eight chartered banks, when that should be the exclusive function of the Bank of Canada, that is what we are opposed to.
Recently, that is on September 23, 1964, without going further, the Montreal newspaper Le Devoir used an eight column headline to trumpet forth that:
Canada Is experiencing a tremendous expansion in money supply credit.
This money supply amounts now to $18,600 million, that is $16,000 million more than the amount of money issued by the Bank of Canada. The Bank of Canada has issued, in round figures, only $2,300 million in paper currency and $230 million in coins, which gives a total of $2,630 million.
Why then is there an $18,600 million money supply? Where does the $14 billion money supply which was not issued by the Bank of Canada come from? That is what the people want to know. Le Devoir points out, through a headline in its financial page, that

f±ie money supply is steadfastly increasing and it uses the speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) to make very interesting remarks. The Minister of Finance may make speeches in Hamilton or elsewhere to praise his department and boast about Canada's finances; he is free to do so. He can have a field day when speaking before people who cannot contradict him or who have no alternative but to accept his statements at face value, but as far as we in the House of Commons are concerned, we, the representatives of the people and not only of big business, as representatives of the people, of every citizen and not only of millionaires who are merely putting up millions of dollars in this country, we-and it is our duty to do so-at least try to throw light on the facts, to bring out the truth, to remove the causes of the economic chaos in which our finances are sinking and will continue to sink year in and year out, even if the Minister of Finance does his utmost to boast everywhere that Canada has never had it so good.
No, Mr. Speaker, Canada is not prosperous, most Canadians are not prosperous, and it is up to us here in parliament to remedy a state of affairs which becomes more intolerable every day. We all have to bear some responsibility for this, at various degrees, but the greatest responsibility rests upon the Minister of Finance. He has already given many signs of his incompetence, but goodwill, I believe, is the only thing he lacks. He could use his intelligence-it is just average but he could still manage-to fairly and shrewdly pinpoint all the faults in our monetary, economic and political systems, the exclusive privileges granted to private banks, and bring about the necessary remedies in due course. But no, as soon as hon. members take the floor, he leaves, he refuses to hear anything, and resumes the remote corners of his lair to meet consultants of foreign countries or representatives of big business who have succeeded in gaining his confidence and who wield their influence on him.
In all those requests for incorporation of banks or finance companies, we are always faced with the same social phenomenon: people everywhere need money. On the one hand, everyone needs money, everywhere at the same time, governments included; on the other hand, small groups of citizens get together to lend money and make profits without making any effort. Others work, build things which are beneficial to the people, but the big profits always go to the financiers, the finance company directors, for the simple
Private Bills
reason that they hold the strings where finance, money and credit are concerned.
That is how the system works. It is not the fault of company directors and chairmen if the system is organized this way and protected by legislation. The 26 ministers are the only ones responsible for the legislation, the administration of that legislation to the distribution of taxes, the control of all monetary, economic and political mechanisms within Canada.
These company officers and directors have always the right to enter into partnership, to ask company, bank or finance company charters. They are not to blame. Anyone of us would like to do the same. Those who are to blame are the government, the ministers who maintain a financing system for the benefit of companies and never in the interest of the human beings living in families.
It is all right for men to take advantage of exclusive privileges granted by the statutes, and they are to be commended for doing so. What must be changed are the provisions in the acts which always favour institutions, by tax exemptions or privileged taxation. The 26 ministers are the only ones responsible for the distribution of taxes and privileges among individuals, families, companies or institutions of all kinds.
Whatever may be the power of pressure groups lobbying ministers and government authorities, it still remains that every citizen has the right to exercise his freedom of speech, his right of association and influence. It rests on members of the government to maintain their position, to act at all times as representatives of the people, protectors of equity and justice, on behalf of the great and the small, the strong and the weak, the rulers and the oppressed.
The rulers, the 26 ministers of the government especially, must above all be the protectors of the weak, the humble folk, the children and the parents less favoured by talent, work, instruction and capital.
The right to live of the individual is the basis of any society. When you see how our ministers are acting as regards the distribution of tax revenues in the society, you would think that only institutions have a right to live, to make profits and to accumulate capital.
Our government ministers are solely responsible for the legal machinery grouping persons to make money to the detriment of the individuals who stand alone against the leaders of society and who cannot make themselves heard to assert their right to live, to

the necessities of life, to freedom, to the protection of their person.
If a man who is educated, rich and a hard worker becomes eventually director of several companies, he is not to be blamed. If he is a good administrator, it is a good thing for himself and for those who make use of his services. But when the companies he administers are not taxed at the same rate as the individuals and when they enjoy privileges in regard to capitalization and profits which are denied to individuals, that is the responsibility of the ministers, particularly of the Minister of Finance and of the top officials of the main departments.
Let us stop seeing guilt every time we see people who know success and make money. It is not the fact that they succeed that is bad. Wealth is a good thing in itself, especially if it is well used. Power is a good thing in itself, especially if it is well used. Science is a good thing in itself, especially if it is put to good use.
Our governments have power, wealth and science, but do they use their power to push up the rich or to crush down the poor? Do they use their power and authority to render justice or to continually patronize the same privileged people who accumulate profits while all the others go into debt, those people who pile up wealth while all the ohers are faced wih increasing hardship?
Mr. Speaker, I would like to be well understood. I want to make myself very clear when I refer to companies, banks and finance institutions.
It is not the men that I rebuke. It is not the managers, the presidents and the directors of these institutions that I rebuke; it is the methods of financing between capital and credit that I find fault with. It is the intermediary system between the individual who works and the one who finances, that I want to improve. It is not because I am a Credi-tiste that I speak like this; it is because I think like this that I am a Creditiste, and this is a personal matter.
I ask you not to consider my words and my interpretations as being those of a group, nor as being those of a founder of the social credit system. I am unable to judge Mr. Douglas' philosophical views, but I am able to judge actions that take place before me every day, every week, every month, in brief the year around; and I can detect whether these actions are good or bad. I can distinguish whether these financial habits are profitable or harmful and whether these methods of disposing of credit, money and capital are beneficial or detrimental to the hard-working

people who make little profit in comparison to these finance administrators who work little but make big profits and earn large incomes.
Once again, even if I were not a Creditiste, even if I were not a member of this house, even if I were only an ordinary Canadian citizen, this is what I would think of this financial system which always enriches those who do no real work and always impoverishes those who truly work, producing something true, real, useful and progressive. Only the financiers, the producers of credit, finance, mortgages, loans can find the way to prosperity, security and control over those who build up the country, who make up the people and the nation.
Make no mistake about it, Mr. Speaker, I am not against the men, presidents, directors or officers, I am not against the experts controlling this system, I am not even against capitalism, the financial system, or the banking system.
I am against certain methods only, against certain privileges being granted to privileged persons; I am against those special favours granted by governments to some companies through tax exemptions, permissions to keep internal, secret and hidden reserves; I am against certain facilities provided to a few individuals and denied to others.
If only I could make myself understood, we could readily understand one another and agree. But a Creditiste member is immediately thought of as an anti-banking theorist. Such is not the case at all. This is not in accordance with the facts. We are perhaps more conventional than most socialistic capitalists, who think they are protecting the present system by allowing it to creep into socialism.
I even think that we are protecting the present capitalist system by striving to remedy its inadequacies, to rid it of its abuses and of some of its methods which are no longer suitable in this age of fast and automatic production.

Mr. Speaker, just when the world is crumbling under the strain of debts and usury, when the provincial legislatures are obliged to propose measures in order to restrict the excessive

exploitation on the part of finance companies in exercising the rights they had obtained under finance company charters, when large labour organizations, labour unions have been campaigning for years so as to caution people against falling prey to those companies, which are taking advantage of them through the interest charged on loans-a great number of consumers are barely able, when they start housekeeping to buy the furniture they need unless through finance companies-just when those finance companies' usurious rates are being denounced from all sides, it is really surprising to find that the other place has so readily approved Bill No. S-13 for the incorporation of a new bank.
Let us pause for a moment and examine the names of the petitioners. Who are those seeking a bank's charter or the incorporation of the Laurentide bank?
It is readily seen that the petitioners hold certain positions in some other branches of our financial system. Are we really trying to make fools of the people who are already hard pressed by usury, by the exorbitant interest charged by finance companies which are exploiting the consumer, the small wage earner, in our Canadian society, when we endeavour to make it easier still, through a bank, for people to take out more short term loans repayable over a period of 12, 18 or 24 months when all those instalment purchases are financed by means of loans requiring no endorsers, if you please? All that is required from the borrowers is a signature on the dotted lines of a contract, of a promissory note showing the amount in favour of the bank holding that promissory note.
We are simply making it easier for that company to multiply, through its own bank, this kind of credit.
What is even more surprising, Mr. Speaker, is that barely a week ago, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) tabled in the house a motion to limit the ability of certain provincial governments to hold existing bank stocks.
It was also said that the measure was intended to prevent foreigners from becoming the main shareholders in our Canadian banks and thus from gaining control of our economy.
Just a glance at the names of the petitioners and of those in key positions suffices to convince us that while they are Canadian residents, they have large interests outside Canada. First of all, there is Mr. Peter Saunders, president of the Laurentide Finance Corporation, president of Coronation Credit, 20220-743

director of the Commonwealth Industrial Bank, in Nassau, and director of Elite Insurance. Then comes Mr. Andrew Elliott Saxton, general manager of the Laurentide Finance Corporation, vice president of the Laurentide Finance Corporation of California, president of Elite Insurance, director of Coronation Credit and director of the Commonwealth Industrial Bank in Nassau. What if all provincial governments were to decide to follow British Columbia's lead, that is to create a charter bank and hold $30 million worth of shares in it?
Others claimed that the Minister of Finance feared precisely the multiplication of chartered banks controlled by a provincial government. We are told that would be something to fear since there would be a Social Credit bank in Alberta, an N.D.P. or socialist bank in Saskatchewan, a Conservative bank in Ontario, a Liberal bank in Quebec and a Conservative bank in Nova Scotia. As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, instead of denying the provinces the right to obtain, under the provisions of the Banks Act of the country, new bank charters even if the Porter commission recommended the creation, the issuing of new charters for additional banks, it would have been more appropriate to study objectively the possibility for the general economy of the country, to issue charters on behalf of certain governments that could use these bank charters to facilitate credit in provinces that need it, and this in order to promote a development more in line with the needs of society.

the premier of British Columbia, who did not want an institution for himself, for his own benefit, but one through which the whole population of that province could have benefited by means of credit made available to certain crown corporations to assist in certain projects such as those provided for in the Columbia river treaty, for they will surely need a tremendous amount of capital to carry out the work required. Other essential projects could also have been financed through the credit which the bank of British Columbia could have made available to various government, municipal and school bodies. There, at last, one could have said: a step forward has been made toward a banking system truly designed to serve the people, and we would have given it our support because it would have been a service institution, instead of the exploiting institution which the Canadian banking system has become.
It is nothing but the exploitation of man by man. And how are you going to refute such an argument?
I have here certain figures on the debt of the Canadian people, taken from the Porter commission's report. That debt stands at $72 billion, that is the total debts of Canadians. That is not a bank debt, but the debts of all Canadians under a system managed by individuals, debts of the community at all government levels.
That is why I am against-rightly so, I think-not only myself personally, but on behalf of my group, to the multiplication and spreading of those chartered banks, especially when petitioners are none other than the directors of finance companies who are already taking unfair advantage of the permission granted to them under a charter which they already hold.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take part very briefly in this discussion and say at the outset of my remarks that I oppose the proposal before us, which is an application for the granting of a charter to set up a private bank in British Columbia, namely the Laurentide bank.

It was agreed, so far as we were concerned, that they would be passed without amendment, but it was not agreed that there would not be brief discussion here and there throughout their passage.
Clause 3 describes the circumstances in which the Canada pension plan will not be operative in any province. In other words, the plan applies in all provinces but under certain circumstances described in clause 3 it will not apply in any province which opts out under the terms of the clause. The point I want to make is that words have been bandied around that this is a universal plan, a national plan, a Canadian plan. In fact its name, the Canada pension plan, seems to imply that under all circumstances it will be a national plan operative in the same way in every part of Canada. It is well for members of the committee and Canadians generally to realize this need not be so.
Clause 3 provides that any province can opt out after due notice, and under the provisions of section 94(a) of the B.N.A. Act all provinces can legislate in this field. The people of Canada should realize that it is not axiomatic and necessarily a fact that this plan will become national in scope and will be completely portable. There is a possibility it might not, and in support of my contention I want to quote Hon. John Robarts, premier of Ontario, in a statement he made to the legislature of Ontario on January 21, 1965. Referring to the question of whether his province was to come into the plan or opt out he said:
In the present circumstances, if we were to propose a plan in which there were any marked differences, even though 'comparable', we might seriously impair the principle of national portability of pensions, which has been one of our goals for many years.
You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that clause 3 provides that a province can opt out provided that within a specified time it passes a bill through its own legislature, establishing a plan with comparable benefits. In effect the premier of Ontario says that if they were to opt out it might impair the national portability of the Canada pension plan. I quote again from his speech, which is to be found at page 1787 of the minutes of the proceedings and evidence of the joint committee:
In coming to this decision-
That is, the decision as to whether or not they should join the Canada pension plan.
-I am well aware that the government of Quebec has indicated that it intends to administer its own pension plan, which will become comparable to the Canada pension plan and, it is hoped, will not seriously impair interprovincial portability.
Canada Pension Plan
I emphasize those words:
-it is hoped, will not seriously impair interprovincial portability. This decision by the province of Quebec is based on the determination of its government to administer its own social welfare legislation. While I can sympathize with this decision, I nevertheless do not despair that in the future the government of Quebec may see fit to enter into the national plan, which will be so similar to its own. If this could come to pass, we would achieve our ultimate goal of a truly national pension plan that would go far toward setting the pattern for future, nation-wide, social welfare legislation.
The object of my brief remarks is to point out that under this bill a province can opt out after due notice and within a certain period of time and, if it does, the Canada pension plan will not, so to speak, become operative in that province if the province at the time of opting out within a specific time passes its own plan which is comparable as far as benefits are concerned. But at any time thereafter, that province or any other province can change its plan in any way it sees fit. This is within their constitutional rights. The people should know this. There is no assurance that the Canada pension plan will be completely national in scope and completely portable. It is true that subsequent clauses in the bill provide for agreements to be entered into between the federal government and a province which may opt out. But such agreements can be made only subsequent to the present bill becoming law and subsequent to the opting out province passing its own legislation. I certainly hope with the best will in the world that this is not the way in which things will turn out. But this is what may happen.
It might have taken a little more time to have arrived by agreement at a plan which would have had a greater chance of becoming a national plan without the possibility of destroying national portability. I believe that what prompted the present approach of the government is its well established policy of co-operative federalism. I believe the attitude taken by the government in establishing this pension plan is in line with its stated policy of allowing provinces to opt out of federal-provincial programs. Had the government not established this policy it might have been possible to have set up a different program, one which would have had greater assurance of being national in its scope. In this regard I should like to quote again one or two of the statements made by the premier of Ontario in his speech before the legislature on January 21, 1965. This indicates the attitude of the premier of On-

Canada Pension Plan
tario toward a national plan. He points out that it is possible for the province of Ontario to opt out and operate its own plan. He said:
With regard to the alternative of operating our own plan, may I say that our studies clearly indicate that it would be entirely feasible for the government of Ontario to do so; indeed, there are substantial arguments in favour of our so doing.
We would then have a plan which could be operated to our satisfaction, both efficiently and economically, for the benefit of the people of this province. We would preserve the constitutional rights which are ours under the British North America Act. We would have complete control over all the funds generated in this province. We would have complete control over any future amendments respecting contributions, benefits and other financial aspects. In addition, although a provincial plan must be comparable to the federal plan, I am convinced that we could make improvements and simplifications in benefits, contributions and administrative features of the plan if we were to devise and operate our own.
In spite of the statement that the people of Ontario could probably benefit by operating their own plan, what did the premier go on to say. He said, in effect, no. These are his words:
The first duty and responsibility of the government of this province is, of course, to look after the interests of our own people. This is our primary objective. On the other hand our position with respect to the whole of Canada and its people is one of which we are proud and which we have traditionally maintained. Thus the decisions we make must be made within the broad context of what is best for the Canadian nation as well as for the province of Ontario.
Mr. Robarts goes on to make other statements along those lines. I maintain in all seriousness that had it not been for the stated policy of this government allowing opting out, it could have been possible even within the constitutional rights of the provinces, indeed it might still be possible, that a truly national plan could be developed.
Remember that a province does not have to state its intention of opting out until this bill has become law. There is a possibility that other provinces may opt out. We know, for instance, that the premier of British Columbia has done many things which have been unexpected in some quarters and it could well be that other provinces would opt out. The premier of Ontario has indicated the real danger to national portability if this were to happen.
I say again that the position taken by this government was predetermined by its policy of allowing any province to opt out, and I hope members of the house and the people of Canada will realize that this is not neces-

sarily a national plan providing for complete portability.

It was impossible to determine how much of a divergency there might be between the federal legislation and the legislation of the province. Accordingly, it was considered that there could be so many computations and permutations that it would be virtually useless at this time to set them down in legislation.
I should like to say, however, that considering the fact that all hon. members of the house have expressed themselves, whatever their political colouration, as being so firmly of the view, as have all provincial groups, that there should be legislation which is portable and universal in its application, I think I can say, even for those dim shadows who may sit in these seats 20, 50 or 100 years from now, that their inclinations for a universal scheme would also be as great, and legislation to fit the circumstances of that time will be readily put through the committee of that day.
